Edmond Michotte wrote the conversation down and published it in 1906. The story belongs with the tales Rossini circulated in old age.

The Fondazione Rossini (Andrea Malnati, January 2026) judges that Rossini met only Beethoven’s brother in 1822 and never met Beethoven. The edge records the legend together with the Foundation’s verdict.

Two days later he wrote that with Beethoven dead only Berlioz could revive him, and sent 20,000 francs through the Baron de Rothschild. He told his librettist Piave that the tragedy was “one of the greatest creations of man” and that if they could not make something great of it they should at least make something out of the ordinary. In 1865 he wrote that Shakespeare was “one of my favorite poets”, whom he had had “in my hands from my earliest youth”. For the revised version, given in French in Paris on 21 April 1865, he insisted that the Witches rule the drama.

works.to: Liszt, Totentanz: Paraphrase on Dies irae, S. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849)

berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.claim: In the finale of the Symphonie fantastique, Berlioz gives the Dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in C minor from bar 127, a funeral rite turned into a parody at the witches’ sabbath. Liszt met Berlioz the day before the premiere on 5 December 1830 and in 1833 made the piano transcription of the symphony. His Totentanz, planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859, is a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant. berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.note: Both works are documented; no letter or statement has been found in which Liszt names the Fantastique as the source of the Dies irae idea. He knew the symphony intimately, but the Pisa fresco is the other recorded stimulus for the Totentanz.

Wagner waited until Vienna in 1861 to see a complete performance. In the meantime he conducted extracts in Zürich, London, Paris and Brussels.

He was soon on intimate terms with the family. Halévy died in March 1862. In June 1869 Bizet married his younger daughter Geneviève, and straight afterwards he paid homage to his father-in-law by completing and revising Halévy’s unfinished opera Noé.

In Reményi’s later telling, Brahms repaid him by falling asleep during Liszt’s B-minor Sonata. The travelling companions parted company; that autumn Brahms called on the Schumanns in Düsseldorf.

Clara’s diary greeted him as a musician “specially sent by God”. works.from: Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1819; 2nd ed. 1844)
works.to: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde (composed 1857–59); letter to Liszt, 16 December 1854

schopenhauer--wagner-letter-to-liszt-185.claim: On 16 December 1854 Wagner wrote from Zürich to Liszt that he had been absorbed in a “gift from heaven”, Arthur Schopenhauer, “the greatest philosopher since Kant”; the poet Georg Herwegh had urged him to read The World as Will and Representation. In the same letter he announces Tristan und Isolde: never having known the true bliss of love, he would “erect a monument to the most beautiful of all my dreams”, a conception he calls the simplest but most full-blooded imaginable, ending under a black flag. The first musical sketches date from 19 December 1856, and on 9 August 1857 he broke off Siegfried to compose it.

gounod--bizet-symphony-in-c-1855.title: Bizet models his Symphony in C on Gounod’s

works.from: Gounod, Symphony No. 1 (1855), arranged by Bizet for piano duet
works.to: Bizet, Symphony in C (autograph dated 29 October–November 1855)

gounod--bizet-symphony-in-c-1855.claim: Hugh Macdonald calls Gounod “certainly the leading influence” on the young Bizet. The works that impressed him most were Sapho (1851), the choruses for Ulysse (1852) and Gounod’s First Symphony (1855). That year Bizet arranged the symphony for piano duet, and just after his seventeenth birthday he wrote his own Symphony in C, which Macdonald calls “clearly” modelled on Gounod’s. The autograph is dated 29 October–November 1855. The score lay forgotten until Felix Weingartner conducted it at Basel on 26 February 1935. In October 1872 Bizet wrote to Gounod: “You were the beginning of my life as an artist. I spring from you.”

works.from: Rossini’s operas, as Bizet knew them in Paris and at the Villa Medici
works.to: Bizet, Clovis et Clotilde (1857) and the Rome envois, 1858–60

rossini--bizet-prix-de-rome-years-1857.claim: The Palazzetto Bru Zane describes Bizet’s Prix de Rome cantata Clovis et Clotilde, performed at the Institut on 3 October 1857, as nourished by the influences of Rossini, Meyerbeer and Gounod. At the Villa Medici, Hugh Macdonald writes, Bizet “had a lively taste for Italian music, especially Rossini”; he preferred Rossini, Mozart and Mendelssohn to Verdi, whose Un ballo in maschera he disliked. For his first Roman envoi he chose an Italian opera over the usual mass. On 25 June 1858 he wrote to his mother that he had found an Italian farce in the style of Don Pasquale and was “decidedly built for comic music”. The result was Don Procopio, an opera buffa wholly in the Italian manner.

rossini--wagner-paris-visit-1860.title: Wagner calls on Rossini in Paris

works.from: Rossini’s conversation with Wagner, Paris, March 1860
works.to: Wagner’s preface to the French prose translation of his opera poems

rossini--wagner-paris-visit-1860.claim: After conducting extracts from his operas in Paris early in 1860, Wagner found a bon mot going round the papers: when Rossini’s friend Mercadante spoke up for Wagner’s music, Rossini had supposedly served him only the sauce of a fish. Rossini denied the story in a public letter, and Wagner called on him. He was received as a friend and heard Rossini say, in a long conversation, that he might have achieved something had he been born and educated in Germany, but that Italy in his youth had left no room for serious aims in opera. Wagner left with the impression of the first truly great man worthy of reverence he had met in the art world, and never saw him again. In the preface to the French prose translation of his opera poems, he wrote, his estimate of modern Italian opera was guided largely by what Rossini had told him from his own experience.

wagner-new-german-school--brahms-manifes.title: Brahms signs against Wagner’s party, then helps Wagner

works.from: The New German School’s organ, Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik; Wagner’s Vienna concerts of 1862–63

wagner-new-german-school--brahms-manifes.claim: In 1860 Brahms and Joseph Joachim signed a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The text leaked, the journal parodied it on 4 May, and the Echo published it two days later with more than twenty names. In Vienna Brahms nevertheless helped prepare Wagner’s concerts of 1862–63 and played him the Handel Variations in January 1863. Wagner gave him part of the Tannhäuser manuscript, then demanded it back in 1875.

wagner-tristan-prelude--berlioz-debats-1.title: Berlioz “reads and re-reads” the Tristan prelude, baffled

works.from: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde, Act I prelude (concert at the Salle Ventadour, February 1860)
works.to: Berlioz, review of Wagner’s concerts, Journal des Débats, 9 February 1860

wagner-tristan-prelude--berlioz-debats-1.claim: Wagner’s Paris concerts of January–February 1860 included the Tristan prelude, and Berlioz reviewed them in the Journal des Débats on 9 February. He describes a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. He says he has read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still cannot tell what the composer means. Wagner, who had sent him the Tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 February.

He wrote the work in a single stretch in September 1861, twenty-five variations and a fugue, and gave it to Clara Schumann on her forty-second birthday, 13 September. When Niedermeyer died in March 1861, saint-saens took charge of piano studies and introduced the pupils to contemporary music, including that of Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Fauré recalled this in old age, and Saint-Saëns remained a lifelong friend; in 1877 he took Fauré to Weimar to meet Liszt.

Thirty years later, in the 1891 preface to his own Principles of Orchestration, he named Berlioz first among the colourists, with Glinka, Liszt and Wagner, who had brought orchestral colour to its zenith. He told students that Weber, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Glinka, Wagner, Liszt and modern French and Russian composers would be their best guides.

berlioz--bizet-pecheurs-de-perles-review.title: Berlioz’s last review praises Bizet’s Pêcheurs de perles

works.from: Berlioz, review in the Journal des débats, 8 October 1863
works.to: Bizet, Les Pêcheurs de perles, Théâtre-Lyrique, 30 September 1863

berlioz--bizet-pecheurs-de-perles-review.claim: Bizet composed Les Pêcheurs de perles in the summer of 1863 for the Théâtre-Lyrique, where it opened on 30 September and ran for eighteen performances. The press condemned the libretto as absurd and the score as noisy and offensive, and Bizet counted the opera a failure. The best notice came from Berlioz, whose review in the Journal des débats on 8 October was his last feuilleton; it recognised the twenty-four-year-old as a serious talent with a great future. Bizet returned the admiration a few weeks later, when the same theatre staged Berlioz’s Les Troyens à Carthage and he offered to fight a duel in its defence.

dargomyzhsky-stone-guest--mussorgsky-mar.claim: Mussorgsky’s idea of setting Gogol’s comedy Marriage came from the advice and example of Alexander Dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began The Stone Guest, declaring that Pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. It replaced the division between aria and recitative with a continuous, syllabic but lyrically heightened declamation. Lyudmila Shestakova gave him a volume of the plays interleaved with blank pages, and he began his libretto in October. He finished the score in December 1869. The Imperial Theatres rejected it on 10 February 1871 by six votes to one; his revised version of 1872 reached the Mariinsky stage on 27 January 1874.

rossini--verdi-messa-per-rossini-1868.claim: Four days after Rossini died, on 17 November 1868, Verdi wrote to his publisher Ricordi proposing that “the most distinguished Italian composers” each set a section of a Requiem Mass for the anniversary of Rossini’s death, to be sealed in the archives of Bologna’s Liceo musicale once it had been performed. Verdi kept his Libera me and revised it for his own Messa da Requiem, first performed at Milan on 22 May 1874.

brahms-hungarian-dances--dvorak-slavonic.claim: Dvořák won the Austrian State Prize in 1874, 1876 and 1877. Brahms, on the committee, referred him to his own publisher, Fritz Simrock, who first issued the Moravian Duets and then asked for something dance-like. Unsure how to begin, Dvořák took Brahms’s Hungarian Dances as a model, but only as a model: Brahms used real Hungarian folk melodies, whereas Dvořák mostly used the characteristic rhythms of Bohemian folk dances with melodies of his own. The Op. 46 set, written for piano four hands, was orchestrated soon after at Simrock’s request.

bizet--tchaikovsky-carmen-letter-1880.title: Tchaikovsky plays through Carmen and predicts its fame

works.to: Tchaikovsky’s letter to Nadezhda von Meck from Simaki, 16–19 July 1880 (Old Style)

bizet--tchaikovsky-carmen-letter-1880.claim: Tchaikovsky was studying the vocal score of Carmen, sent to him by Vladimir Shilovsky, by mid-1875, and heard the opera for the first time at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 20 January 1876, with Célestine Galli-Marié in the title role. By the start of 1878 he had learnt almost the whole of it by heart. In July 1880, staying at Nadezhda von Meck’s cottage at Simaki, he told her that to rest from his own music he had played Carmen through from beginning to end. To his mind it was a masterpiece “in the full sense” of the word, one of the few works fated to reflect most strongly the musical aspirations of a whole age. He was convinced that within ten years it would be the most popular opera in the world.

bizet--nietzsche-carmen-genoa-1881.claim: On 27 November 1881 Friedrich Nietzsche heard Carmen for the first time, at the Politeama Theatre in Genoa. He wrote to his sister that he had been thunderstruck by an opera “so strong, so impassioned, so graceful, so Southern”, and he heard it again five days later. In The Case of Wagner (1888) he wrote that he had just heard Bizet’s masterpiece “for the twentieth time”, that Bizet’s orchestration was the only one he could still endure, and that this music was light and definite and free of grimaces, the opposite of Wagner’s “endless melody”.

larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.claim: At the end of 1891 Sibelius travelled with the aesthetician Yrjö Hirn to Porvoo to hear the Izhorian rune singer Larin Paraske. Sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses Finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. Kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the Kalevala, followed in 1892.
larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.note: Hirn’s recollection and Sibelius’s own account place a hearing at Porvoo at the end of 1891, while Sibelius later claimed he first met Paraske on his 1892 honeymoon in Lieksa. That he heard her is documented; where and when he first did is not settled, and how far her singing shaped Kullervo is interpretation.

nadia-boulanger--copland-fontainebleau-1.claim: In May 1921 Copland enrolled at the newly established American Conservatory at Fontainebleau. A friend urged him to attend the harmony class of a young Frenchwoman, Nadia Boulanger. He later remembered hesitating, “because I had never heard of any composer who had studied with a woman”, but he chose her as his teacher and began composition studies with her in October. A year of study in France became three. In 1924 Boulanger took him to meet Koussevitzky in Paris; after hearing part of Copland’s ballet Grohg at the piano, the conductor ordered an organ concerto for Boulanger to play. It became the Symphony for Organ and Orchestra, which she played in New York in 1925 under Walter Damrosch. “I don’t know what my career would have been like without her!” Copland often said.

Under Price’s tutelage, Arionne Nettles writes, Bonds went on to become one of the great composers of the Chicago Black Renaissance.

schoenberg--cage-lessons-1935.title: Cage studies with Schoenberg in Los Angeles

works.from: Schoenberg’s analysis, counterpoint and composition classes, Los Angeles, from 18 March 1935

schoenberg--cage-lessons-1935.claim: Prepared by Henry Cowell and Adolph Weiss, John Cage asked Schoenberg to teach him. Schoenberg warned that he probably could not afford his price; Cage said he had no money, and when he answered yes to the question whether he would devote his life to music, Schoenberg taught him free of charge. From 18 March 1935 Cage studied analysis in small group sessions at Schoenberg’s Hollywood home, and he also attended a private counterpoint class and classes in composition, harmony and counterpoint at the University of Southern California and then at UCLA. After two years it was clear to both of them, Cage remembered, that he had no feeling for harmony, which for Schoenberg was structural. “You’ll come to a wall and won’t be able to get through,” Schoenberg told him. “Then I’ll spend my life knocking my head against that wall,” Cage answered. At the Cornish School in Seattle he made what he called his response to Schoenberg’s structural harmony: a rhythmic structure in which the large parts of a piece have the same proportion as the phrases of a single unit.

Copland invited him to his birthday party that night and began a correspondence in which he wrote as counsellor and addressed him as “Dear Pupil”. The first published works under his name were the solo and two-piano arrangements of El Salón México that Copland asked him to make. In the 1940s he conducted many of the early performances of the Third Symphony and cut a few bars from its finale on his own initiative. Copland came to agree: it was the only change, Vivian Perlis writes, that he ever accepted.

He added the fiddle tunes “Hop Light Ladies” and “Gilderoy”. The Library of Congress’s account is that Copland probably never heard the field recording. The Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo gave Rodeo its first performance in New York on 16 October 1942.

satie--cage-black-mountain-festival-1948.claim: John Cage came to know the music of Satie in Paris in 1930, and it stayed a lifelong source of inspiration. Teaching at Black Mountain College in July and August 1948, he found its largely German community unfamiliar with Satie and organised a festival of twenty-five concerts, each with short introductions of his own. In the middle he placed a lecture, Defense of Satie, that set Satie against Beethoven and found Satie right; it caused a controversy. The festival included Satie’s play Le Piège de Méduse, with Buckminster Fuller as Baron Méduse and Elaine de Kooning as Frisette, and Merce Cunningham danced the “Monkey Dances” as Jonas to Cage’s prepared piano. In 1949 Cage published Satie’s Vexations, found in Henri Sauguet’s private collection, in Contrepoints (Paris, no. 6). On 9–10 September 1963 he initiated the first complete performance, at the Pocket Theatre in New York: eighteen hours and forty minutes, with a relay of ten pianists.

tristan-chord.name: The Tristan chord
tristan-chord.summary: F–B–D♯–G♯ sounds in bar 2 of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde prelude. The chord promises a resolution that the music keeps postponing. Its four notes came to stand for longing itself, ready for later composers to quote with devotion or a sly smile.

lament-bass.name: The lament bass
lament-bass.summary: The bass falls through a fourth and starts again. In Purcell’s When I am laid in earth, it fills the descent from G to D with every semitone while Dido sings her farewell. Her phrases change; the bass keeps coming back.

la-folia.name: La Folia
la-folia.summary: An old dance tune and a familiar round of chords leave plenty of room for mischief. Vivaldi begins his Folia in D minor, the first violin stepping slowly through the tune. The variations soon set the fingers running.

ode-to-joy.name: Ode to Joy
ode-to-joy.summary: Beethoven’s tune begins with two repeated notes, climbs by step and comes back down. It carries Schiller’s appeal to human fellowship into the Ninth Symphony’s finale. That plain, singable line has travelled through piano transcriptions and public ceremonies far beyond the concert hall.

frere-jacques.name: Frère Jacques
frere-jacques.summary: The familiar round enters Mahler’s First Symphony on a solo double bass, in D minor, over the timpani’s tread. Frère Jacques still repeats its little phrases, but now they belong to a funeral procession. The bassoon and cellos join the round.
